## TL;DR

Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) from farms deposits reactive nitrogen downwind, and where plants are short of nitrogen the extra supply adds leaf. More leaf does two things to ozone at once: it pulls ozone out of the air through stomata, and it emits more isoprene, which makes ozone where $\text{NO}_x$ is abundant. In our global model study[^4], this leaf effect alone moved surface ozone by no more than about $\pm 0.5\text{ ppbv}$; larger changes came from extra soil $\text{NO}_x$ ($+1$ to $+3\text{ ppbv}$ in some low-$\text{NO}_x$ equatorial regions) and from vegetation-driven changes in weather (within $\pm 2$–$3\text{ ppbv}$ in summer). After this module you can explain why the leaf effect can take either sign, and why it was not the largest term in that study.
:::

## From farm ammonia to forest canopy

Three steps link a fertilised field to a forest canopy downwind:

1. **Agricultural ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) emissions**: fertiliser and livestock release ammonia gas. The inventory used in our study puts year-2000 emissions at about $53\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ ($71 - 18$; 53 million tonnes of nitrogen), rising to $71\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ by 2050 under a business-as-usual scenario[^4].
2. **Transport and wet/dry deposition**: much of the nitrogen humans fix is lost to air, water and land[^1]. Winds carry reactive nitrogen from ammonia (and from $\text{NO}_x$) downwind, and it returns to land and ocean by wet and dry deposition; as ammonia grows and $\text{NO}_x$ is regulated, deposition is projected to shift from nitrate ($\text{NO}_3^-$) towards ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$)[^4].
3. **Vegetation response**: where soils are nitrogen-limited, the deposited nitrogen acts as fertiliser and can raise plant growth, canopy density (**leaf area index, LAI**) and canopy height. Where soils already have more nitrogen than plants can use, it adds little growth[^4].

### The dry deposition sink

Ozone exchange between ecosystems and the air is a long-studied surface-exchange problem[^2]. Ground-level ozone is removed at the surface through **stomatal uptake** and destruction on other canopy surfaces, usually written as a flux through resistances in series:

$$F_{\text{dry}} = -v_d [\text{O}_3] = -\frac{1}{R_a + R_b + R_c} [\text{O}_3]$$

where $R_c$ is canopy resistance. More leaf area ($\text{LAI}$) means more stomata, which lowers $R_c$, raises $v_d$ and removes ozone faster. The model in our study uses this resistance-in-series scheme with stomatal resistance tied to LAI[^4].

### The biogenic VOC source

Plants emit **isoprene** ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$), monoterpenes and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs); MEGAN2.1 estimates global biogenic VOC emission at about $1\text{ Pg yr}^{-1}$, about half of it isoprene[^3]. In our study's model, MEGAN2.1 computes these emissions as functions of LAI, leaf temperature, sunlight and soil moisture, so more leaf means more isoprene[^4]. In sunlight, with $\text{NO}_x$ present, isoprene feeds ozone production:

$$\text{Isoprene} + \text{OH} + \text{NO}_x + h\nu \to \text{Peroxy Radicals} \to \text{Tropospheric }\text{O}_3$$

Where anthropogenic $\text{NO}_x$ is abundant (a VOC-limited regime; see [NOx, VOCs and sunlight](/blogs/nox-vocs-and-sunlight.html)), extra isoprene adds ozone. Earlier studies summarised in our paper describe the same two-way pull: more LAI can raise ozone through biogenic VOCs in high-$\text{NO}_x$ air and lower it through stomatal uptake[^4].

## What the coupled model shows

In our study in *Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics*[^4], we ran a global model with year-2000 and year-2050 agricultural ammonia emissions. Nitrogen deposition rose by $20\%$ ($20\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$), and LAI rose by $0.1$–$0.2\text{ m}^2\text{ m}^{-2}$ across midlatitude boreal and temperate forests and by up to $0.3$–$0.4\text{ m}^2\text{ m}^{-2}$ over tropical grasslands and croplands. We then switched each land change on separately, first with meteorology held fixed ("prescribed") and then with weather free to respond ("dynamic"). The two-pathway leaf effect turned out to be the smallest of the terms:

| Change switched on (meteorology) | Summer surface $\text{O}_3$ change | Where and why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Leaf area index only** (prescribed) | within $\pm 0.5\text{ ppbv}$ | Isoprene and deposition partly cancel; isoprene dominated in northern midlatitude regions with low LAI to begin with |
| **Canopy height only** (prescribed) | about $-0.2\text{ ppbv}$ | Taller canopy, more turbulent mixing, faster dry deposition |
| **Soil $\text{NO}_x$ only**, $7.9 \to 8.7\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ (prescribed) | $+1$ to $+3\text{ ppbv}$ | Some low-$\text{NO}_x$ equatorial regions; $80$–$90\%$ of the prescribed-meteorology total |
| **All changes** (dynamic) | within $\pm 2$–$3\text{ ppbv}$ | Vegetation shifts surface energy balance, moisture and circulation; e.g. increases in the central–eastern USA |

All numbers in the table are from the paper's full text[^4]. It is one model, a business-as-usual emission scenario the paper calls worst-case, and it leaves out ozone damage to plants; treat the magnitudes as one estimate, not a settled range.

### Explore the regime dependence

Change the chemical regime and the deposition surge to see which term wins. This is a toy: its linear coefficients were chosen by hand to illustrate the sign change and are not output from the paper. At the default $40\%$ setting it gives $-0.84$ to $+0.60\text{ ppb}$, already larger than the paper's leaf-only signal of about $\pm 0.5\text{ ppbv}$.

::: {.sim-card}
#### Forest nitrogen-deposition ozone toy model

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ndep = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 40, step: 5, label: "Nitrogen deposition surge (%)"})
viewof regime = Inputs.select(new Map([
  ["Remote Rural (NOx-Limited)", "nox-lim"],
  ["Suburban Transition Zone", "trans"],
  ["Polluted Megacity Margin (VOC-Limited)", "voc-lim"]
]), {value: "nox-lim", label: "Atmospheric chemical regime"})

// The downstream gains are chained off the *rounded* LAI figure, as the
// original widget did, so the displayed numbers stay identical.
laiGain = Number((ndep * 0.16).toFixed(1))
vdGain = (laiGain * 0.9).toFixed(1)
vocGain = (laiGain * 1.12).toFixed(1)

o3 = {
  if (regime === "nox-lim") {
    const d = -(ndep * 0.021);
    return {text: d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#38bdf8",
      note: "NOx-limited remote forest (toy setting): extra stomatal uptake outweighs the extra isoprene, so net surface ozone falls."};
  }
  if (regime === "trans") {
    const d = ndep * 0.003;
    return {text: (d >= 0 ? "+" : "") + d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#f59e0b",
      note: "Transition zone (toy setting): the deposition sink and the isoprene source nearly cancel, so net surface ozone barely moves."};
  }
  const d = ndep * 0.015;
  return {text: "+" + d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#ef4444",
    note: "VOC-limited urban fringe (toy setting): abundant anthropogenic NOx turns the extra isoprene into ozone, so net surface ozone rises."};
}

</div>`

  ${card(html`Deposition Velocity (<i>v</i><sub>d</sub>)`, "+" + vdGain + "%", "#38bdf8")}
  ${card("Isoprene Emission Flux", "+" + vocGain + "%", "#f59e0b")}
  ${card("Net Surface O₃ Response", o3.text, o3.colour)}
</div>`
```

### Data and code

- **Atmosphere and chemistry**: the **Community Earth System Model (CESM) 1.2.2**, with CAM4 coupled to CAM-Chem (MOZART-4 tropospheric chemistry)[^4].
- **Land**: **Community Land Model 4.5**, run with active carbon–nitrogen biogeochemistry to get the vegetation and soil responses, then with those changes prescribed in the ozone runs (asynchronous coupling). Biogenic emissions come from MEGAN2.1[^3]^,^[^4].
- **Data**: the paper states that model output can be obtained from the corresponding author on request; it does not link a public code repository[^4].

## Key takeaways

- Agricultural ammonia can act as a fertiliser downwind, but only where soils are nitrogen-limited. In our model, LAI rose by $0.1$–$0.2\text{ m}^2\text{ m}^{-2}$ in midlatitude forests, with little growth response in nitrogen-saturated regions such as India and northern China[^4].
- More leaf strengthens both an ozone sink (stomatal dry deposition, lower $R_c$) and an ozone source (isoprene emission). Regime chemistry suggests the local $\text{NO}_x$ level helps decide which wins; in our model the isoprene term dominated where LAI was low to begin with[^4].
- In that study the leaf effect alone was small (within $\pm 0.5\text{ ppbv}$). Soil $\text{NO}_x$ ($+1$ to $+3\text{ ppbv}$ in some low-$\text{NO}_x$ regions) and vegetation-driven weather changes (within $\pm 2$–$3\text{ ppbv}$) mattered more[^4].
- My inference: models that hold deposition velocities and biogenic emissions fixed cannot represent this link between agricultural emissions and ozone, though how much that matters is not settled by one model study.
- My inference, not tested in the paper: where ozone near farmland is VOC-limited, cutting $\text{NO}_x$ should also reduce how much extra biogenic isoprene becomes ozone.
